doc.title: Carmen Leggio interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Big band economics and unpaid engagements
summary: Bands struggle on the road; Woody Herman waited months to be paid after a Basin Street West job; estate bands do well.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: I can’t imagine what some of those fellows, like in the Basie band and so forth, they did that for so many years.

They lived on the road. Yeah. They lived on the road. Now for instance like the Glenn Miller band, people like that, they are living by the estate. So the band stays busy all the time. They’re probably making good money but they have to stay on the road, you know. But the original bands — I was out on the west coast with Woody Herman at the Basin Street West right, I did two weeks there. And when it came time, the engagement was over with, the owners left, disappeared. And so Woody, we had to wait to get paid, maybe about seven, eight months later. That’s the kind of thing. They just disappeared.
But the Glenn Miller band has no trouble because they’re going by the estate you know.
I don’t know, the Basie band is out there, I guess they’re doing good you know, I don’t know too much about them.
